newsitem.title: USA: Mass Gov Weld submits less controversial budget.
newsitem.headline: Mass Gov Weld submits less controversial budget.

text.p: Massachusetts Gov William Weld on Wednesday submitted an $18.2 billion budget for fiscal 1998 that is much less ambitious than his budget for the previous year, which included dramatic cutbacks and restructurings.

"We decided to go hunting where the ducks are as opposed to firing scatter shots, Number eight, into the air," Weld told reporters at a news conference. He explained he had targeted the new plan to items that were most likely to win approval from the legislature to avoid re-debating issues.

The Republican governor's budget calls for increasing spending by 2.9 percent, with most of the extra funds going towards education reform, phasing out the Lottery Cap, and aid for cities and towns, which will total $3.8 billion.
Seven tax cuts, which would be worth $81 million in fiscal 1998, would be handed out to taxpayers and businesses, but Weld sees no problem in paying for them.
"I can say to the legislature with a straight face that we can afford all seven of the tax cuts and still expand the programs we are expanding," he said.

Massachusetts is expected to end its 1997 fiscal year with an over $100 million surplus, which will help fund another $85 million income tax cut for fiscal 1998 that top lawmakers and the Weld Administration agreed to in mid-January.

The new list of cuts includes a $3,500 job training tax credit for employers, phasing out over five years the 12 percent tax on unearned income to 5.95 percent, as well as tax breaks for the telecommunications industry and domestic insurance companies.

Spurred by a recent default on $4.7 million of notes by Middlesex County, Weld renewed his campaign to abolish county governments, saying the state might be able to produce long-term savings by taking over many of the counties' functions.

Capital spending was budgeted at around $2.9 billion, a sum Lowell Richards, assistant secretary for capital resources, said was basically level with the previous year, and which includes $1.5 billion of federal funds for transportation improvements.

Programs to spend $125 million on environmental remediation and improving and repairing public buildings and another $583 million on renovating and acquiring courthouses will be paid for with bonds that will be sold in the next five to 10 years, Richards said.
The state is subject to an approximately $900 million annual debt limit.

The governor also recommended selling $200 million of general obligation bonds and Massachusetts Land Bank bonds to pay for converting Fort Devens, located about 50 miles west of Boston in Havard, Ayer and Shirley, to a civilian complex.
